questions.question: What is a service in Angular, and how does dependency injection work?
questions.title: Angular Services and Dependency Injection
questions.direct_answer: A service is a TypeScript class (decorated with @Injectable) that holds shared logic or data (fetching, state, business rules) that components shouldn't duplicate. Dependency injection (DI) is Angular's mechanism for giving a component the services it needs: you declare a service as a provider, and when a component's constructor asks for it, Angular creates (or reuses) the instance and injects it. providedIn: 'root' makes a service a singleton app-wide. DI makes components lean (they delegate to services) and makes services mockable in tests — the core of maintainable Angular code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand a service as shared logic and DI as Angular constructing and injecting it into components — and that providedIn: 'root' means singleton.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting data-fetching or business logic directly in a component instead of a service (untestable, duplicated).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: A service is @Injectable shared logic; DI injects it into components via constructor; providedIn:'root' = singleton. Components stay lean; services are mockable.

sections.title: Services Hold Shared Logic; DI Wires It
sections.content: A service in Angular is a TypeScript class decorated with @Injectable that holds shared logic or data — fetching from an API, holding cart state, or enforcing business rules — that components shouldn't duplicate. Dependency injection (DI) is how Angular hands a component the services it needs: you register a service as a provider, and when a component's constructor asks for it, Angular creates (or reuses) the instance and injects it automatically. Setting providedIn: 'root' makes a service a singleton across the whole app. DI lets components stay lean — they delegate to services — and makes services mockable in tests, which is the foundation of maintainable Angular code.

sections.title: How DI Wires a Service to a Component
sections.content:
The component asks for a service in its constructor; Angular resolves the provider and injects the (singleton) instance.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Provider: CartService providedIn: root] -->|singleton| I[(CartService instance)]
  C[CartComponent constructor] -->|asks for| I
  I -.injected into.-> C
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Putting fetch/business logic directly in a component instead of a service — duplicated and untestable.
Forgetting @Injectable on a service, or not setting providedIn so it can't be injected.
Creating a service instance with new instead of letting Angular inject it (loses the singleton/DI).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A service is an @Injectable class holding shared logic/data; DI is how Angular injects it into components.
Register a service (providedIn:'root' = singleton app-wide); components ask for it in the constructor.
DI keeps components lean (delegate to services) and makes services mockable in tests.
Don't new up a service — let Angular inject it to preserve singleton and testability.
Services are the backbone of maintainable Angular: logic lives in services, components stay thin.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: A service in Angular is a TypeScript class decorated with Injectable that holds shared logic or data — fetching from an API, holding cart state, or enforcing business rules — that components shouldn't duplicate. Dependency injection is how Angular hands a component the services it needs. You register a service as a provider, and when a component's constructor asks for it, Angular creates or reuses the instance and injects it automatically. Setting providedIn root makes a service a singleton across the whole app, so every component gets the same instance and shared state. DI lets components stay lean — they delegate to services — and makes services mockable in tests, which is the foundation of maintainable Angular code. The common mistakes are putting fetch or business logic directly in a component instead of a service, forgetting the Injectable decorator, or creating a service with new instead of letting Angular inject it, which loses the singleton and testability.
